## The idea

Play C major as C-E-G, then move C above G. The pitch classes remain C, E, and G,
yet the second chord feels lighter and less settled. The lowest note changes the
chord's weight even when its harmonic identity survives.

An *inversion* moves one or more low chord tones up an octave. A *voicing* is the
specific register and spacing chosen for every tone. Root position puts the root
in the bass; first inversion puts the third there; second inversion puts the
fifth there. These are data transformations over an ordered pitch array.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 78
use_synth :piano

define :invert do |notes, count|
  result = notes.sort
  count.times { result = result.drop(1) + [result[0] + 12] }
  result
end

define :distance do |left, right|
  left.zip(right).sum { |a, b| (a - b).abs }
end

define :voice_near do |notes, previous|
  candidates = (0..2).map { |turn| invert(notes, turn) }
  shifted = candidates.flat_map do |candidate|
    [-12, 0, 12].map { |shift| candidate.map { |pitch| pitch + shift } }
  end
  shifted.min_by { |candidate| distance(candidate, previous) }
end

c = chord(:c4, :major).to_a
[c, invert(c, 1), invert(c, 2), [48, 67, 76]].each do |voicing|
  play_chord voicing, release: 1.3
  sleep 2
end

roots = [:c4, :a3, :f3, :g3]
previous = c
roots.each do |root|
  raw = chord(root, :major).to_a
  chosen = voice_near(raw, previous)
  puts "#{root}: #{chosen} movement=#{distance(chosen, previous)}"
  play_chord chosen, release: 1.5
  sleep 2
  previous = chosen
end
```

The first three chords cycle through bass notes while preserving their pitch
classes. The widely spaced fourth chord opens a large gap around the middle.
The progression then chooses nearby inversions, keeping each new chord in the
same region rather than jumping with its written root.

## Change one thing

1. Play the progression with `raw` instead of `chosen`. Compare the bass leaps
   with the version selected by `voice_near`.
2. Remove `-12` and `12` from the shift list. The search space shrinks, and some
   transitions can no longer find their nearest register.
3. Replace `[48, 67, 76]` with `[60, 64, 67]`. Both describe C major pitch
   classes, but the close version occupies one compact band.

## Why it works

Inversion treats a chord as a cyclic ordering with octave correction. Moving the
first element to the end would lower the order unless twelve semitones were
added. The result preserves each value modulo twelve.

Voicing adds register as another decision. `voice_near` generates candidates,
scores each by total semitone movement from the previous chord, and chooses the
minimum. This greedy search has no knowledge of musical style. It can still
remove glaring leaps because the cost function encodes a useful preference.

The lowest pitch deserves separate attention. A minimum-distance chord may place
an unstable chord tone in the bass. Later voice leading will add constraints for
range, crossing, and common tones. The current function exposes the mechanism
without pretending one numeric score settles every arrangement choice.

Octave equivalence makes the candidate search finite only because the program
sets a register window. Without the three shifts, infinitely many copies of each
pitch class would be available. Real instruments impose ranges, and arrangements
usually assign a working band to each part. Encoding those bounds turns a vague
preference for nearby notes into a reproducible search space.

## Take it further

Extend `voice_near` with a `bass_pitch_class` argument. Reject candidates whose
lowest note has another pitch class. Use it to render C, F, G, C with C and F in
root position, G in first inversion, and the final C in second inversion. Keep
total movement below the root-position version and print both totals.
